passage:
In their Nairobi flat, Zanele's voice got louder and louder. "You never let me go anywhere! Everyone else is going to Amani's party!"
Her mother Wanjiru's voice rose too. "Because it ends at midnight and nobody's parents will be there!"
"You don't trust me!" Zanele was shouting now, her throat raw. "You never listen!"
She stopped. Her hands were shaking. This was going nowhere.
"I need a break," she said, much quieter, and walked out to the balcony. She stood there breathing in the cool air, watching the matatus below.
Ten minutes later, she went back in. Her mother was sitting at the table. Zanele sat opposite. "Can we talk without shouting? I just want you to hear why it matters to me."
Wanjiru nodded slowly. "I'm listening."

qa.q: Where did Zanele go to take a break?
qa.a: Out to the balcony.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling while she shouted?
qa.a: Zanele felt frustrated and hurt, wanting her mother to hear her and trust her.

qa.q: Which choice of Zanele's worked, and why?
qa.a: Taking a break on the balcony and coming back to talk in a lower voice worked, because it stopped the argument escalating and got her mother listening.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru have felt when Zanele came back calmly?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably felt relieved and more willing to listen, since the shouting had stopped.

grounding: A teenager yells in a quarrel with her mother, then takes a break and returns to talk quietly, which works better.

At the school council meeting, Samir and Trisha were arguing about the annual day budget. It started calm, but soon they were both shouting across the table.
"You always take the sports side!" Trisha yelled.
"And you only care about the dance!" Samir shouted back.
Other members went quiet. The teacher in charge, Mr Kulkarni, raised a hand. "Let's take a five-minute break."
Samir walked out to the corridor and leaned against the wall, breathing hard. Trisha stayed in the room, arms crossed.
When they came back, Samir spoke first, quietly. "Sorry. I got loud. Can we split it and try both?"
Trisha let out a breath. "Okay. I was loud too."
They worked it out in fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How long a break did Mr Kulkarni call?
qa.a: A five-minute break.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he shouted across the table?
qa.a: Samir felt frustrated and unheard, believing Trisha only cared about the dance.

qa.q: How did the break help the argument?
qa.a: It gave both of them time to calm down, so they could return with lower voices and find a compromise.

qa.q: How might the other members have felt during the shouting?
qa.a: They probably felt uncomfortable and tense, which is why they went quiet.

grounding: At a school council meeting, two teenagers shout, take a break, and return to talk calmly, finding a solution.

During today's English class, Ankita kept clearing her throat every few minutes. Yusuf, sitting in front, turned around twice and glared. After his answer about the poem, she cleared her throat again, and he said loudly, "If you think my answer's stupid, just say it!"
The class went silent. Ankita looked shocked.

She nodded. "I've had a cold since Saturday. I'm really sorry, Yusuf. It's not about you."
Yusuf's face went red. "Oh. Sorry."
I gave Ankita water and let her sit near the window. I reminded the class that sounds like this can have many reasons.
- Mrs Joseph

The choir concert was tomorrow, and there was no time to change parts. At the final rehearsal, Ojas opened his mouth for the high note, and his voice cracked, a loud squeak, then a low croak.
A couple of kids snickered. Ojas went red and stopped singing.
Avni, standing next to him, kept her eyes on the music and didn't laugh. She whispered, "Keep going. Nobody cares."
The music teacher, Mrs Pinto, stopped the piano. "Ojas, that's your voice changing. It happens to everyone. It's physical, not nerves. It'll settle with time."
"But the concert's tomorrow!"
"Then sing the lower line tonight. I'll switch you."
Ojas let out a breath. Avni nudged him. "See?"
He sang the lower line, and it came out smooth.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pinto suggest Ojas sing?
qa.a: The lower line.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: Ojas felt embarrassed and worried, especially with the concert the next day.

qa.q: What did Avni and Mrs Pinto do that helped?
qa.a: Avni ignored the crack and encouraged him, and Mrs Pinto explained the change was physical and switched his part.

qa.q: How might the kids who snickered see Ojas's voice crack after Mrs Pinto's explanation?
qa.a: They might realise it's a normal body change, not something to laugh at.

grounding: Before a concert, a teenager's voice cracks, a friend ignores it, and a teacher reassures it will settle.

passage:
At a family dinner in their Bengaluru flat, Yogesh was telling a story about his cricket match. Mid-sentence, his voice cracked, jumping high then dropping.
His cousin Rohit burst out laughing. "Did you just squeak?"
Yogesh went silent, face burning.
His sister Indu didn't laugh. She said calmly, "So what happened after the catch?"
Yogesh took a breath and finished his story, voice still wobbly.
Later, Papa found him on the balcony. "Your voice is changing. That's your body growing. Mine did the same at your age."
"Everyone laughed."
"Only Rohit. And his cracked too, two years ago. It settles with time."
Yogesh smiled a little. "Really?"
"Really. Ask Rohit."

qa.q: What was Yogesh telling a story about?
qa.a: His cricket match.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when his cousin laughed?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and ashamed, his face burning.

qa.q: What did Indu do that helped?
qa.a: Indu ignored the crack and asked a question to help Yogesh continue his story.

qa.q: How did Papa help Yogesh understand?
qa.a: Papa explained the voice change was physical, part of growing, and that it would settle with time.

grounding: At a family dinner, a teenager's voice cracks, a sister ignores it, and a parent reassures it's physical and temporary.

passage:
"Damini Didi, why does my voice keep doing this?" Omkar's voice cracked on "this," going from high to low.
"Doing what?"
"That! The squeaky thing!"
"Oh, Omkar." Damini put down her book. "It's your voice changing. Your throat is growing, and it takes time to settle."
"But it's so embarrassing. In class, everyone looks at me when it happens."
"Does anyone laugh?"
"Sometimes. Mostly my friends ignore it."
"Good friends. It's not about feelings, it's just your body. It happened to your Bhaiya too, remember?"
Omkar thought about it. "He used to sound like a donkey."
Damini laughed. "Exactly. And now he sings at weddings."
"Okay," Omkar said, and his voice cracked again. This time he laughed.

qa.q: Whose voice used to sound like a donkey, according to Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar's Bhaiya.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling about his voice cracking?
qa.a: Omkar felt embarrassed, especially when classmates looked at him when it happened.

qa.q: How did Damini reassure Omkar?
qa.a: She explained the cracking is a physical change that settles with time and reminded him of his brother's voice.

qa.q: How do Omkar's friends respond to the cracks?
qa.a: His friends mostly ignore it, which Damini points out is kind.

grounding: A teenager asks an older cousin about his cracking voice, and she reassures him it's physical and will settle.

passage:
In the small village school, results day was loud with children crowding the noticeboard. Usha had topped the district, and Ramesh Sir asked her to say a few words to the class.
She stood up. "Thank you, Sir. Next year I'll be going to a school in the city..." Her voice caught. She cleared her throat, clipped the rest of the words short. "So. Thank you."
She sat down quickly, staring at her desk.
Ramesh Sir didn't ask her to continue. After class, he waited by the door. "Usha, would you like to sit in the staff room for a minute? It's quiet there."
She nodded. In the empty room, she finally said, "I'll miss everyone. I'll miss this school."
Sir nodded. "We'll miss you too. That's why it's hard to say."

qa.q: What had Usha achieved in the results?
qa.a: She had topped the district.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when her voice caught?
qa.a: Usha felt sad and emotional about leaving her village school and friends.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He didn't press her to finish in public and offered a private, quiet moment in the staff room.

qa.q: How might the class have seen Usha's short speech?
qa.a: They might have thought she was shy or in a hurry, not realising she was holding back tears.

grounding: In a village school, a teenager hides a choked voice when speaking, and a teacher offers a private moment instead of pressing.

passage:
In their Sydney classroom, Mr Tuan asked each student to share their weekend. When it was Soo-ah's turn, she started, "My dog, Bori..." Her voice cracked. She cleared her throat hard and said quickly, "He's gone. Pass."
The class went quiet. A few kids looked at her, curious.
Mr Tuan nodded. "Thank you, Soo-ah. We'll move on." He called the next student.
After class, he found her by her locker. "I'm really sorry about Bori. Do you want to talk about him, just the two of us?"
Soo-ah's eyes filled. "He was fourteen. I've had him since I was a baby."
Mr Tuan listened. "That's a long time to love someone. Take your time."
She wiped her eyes and told him about Bori.

qa.q: How old was Bori?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she said "Pass"?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt deep grief over losing Bori and was trying to hide her choked voice in front of the class.

qa.q: What did Mr Tuan do that helped?
qa.a: He didn't press Soo-ah in public, moved on quickly, and offered a private conversation later.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Soo-ah's quick "Pass"?
qa.a: Some might have been curious or confused, not knowing how much she was hurting.

grounding: A teenager clips her words to hide a choked voice about her dog, and a teacher offers a private moment instead of pressing.

passage:
At the village school assembly, it was Darshan's turn to lead the morning prayer. Halfway through the first line, his voice cracked, a high squeak and then a deep rumble.
A few children in the front row giggled.
Darshan paused. His ears went hot. He almost stopped.
Then he saw Gurleen, standing in the second row, looking straight ahead as if nothing had happened.
He grinned, shrugged, and said into the mic, "Sorry, my voice is changing gears." A few people laughed with him. He started the line again and finished the prayer.
Afterwards, Gurleen said, "Nobody will remember the crack. They'll remember the joke."
Darshan laughed. "Changing gears. I'm keeping that one."

qa.q: What did Darshan say into the mic after his voice cracked?
qa.a: "Sorry, my voice is changing gears."

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when the children giggled?
qa.a: Darshan felt embarrassed, his ears going hot, and he almost stopped.

qa.q: What helped Darshan keep going?
qa.a: Seeing Gurleen ignore the crack and making a light joke about it helped him laugh it off and finish.

qa.q: How did Gurleen see the voice crack?
qa.a: Gurleen treated it as nothing important, ignoring it and later saying people would remember the joke.

grounding: In a village school assembly, a teenager's voice cracks, a friend ignores it, and he laughs it off instead of going silent.

passage:
In a Lisbon classroom, Paulo raised his hand to answer the geography question. "The capital of Australia is Can—" His voice squeaked high on "Can" and dropped low on "berra."
Paulo froze.
A couple of boys snorted. Selin, at the next desk, didn't even look up from her notebook, as if nothing had happened.
Paulo took a breath and laughed. "Canberra. With special effects."
The class laughed, this time with him. The teacher smiled. "Correct. Special effects included."
Later Selin said, "I didn't even notice."
"You did," Paulo said.
"Okay, I did. But it didn't matter."

qa.q: What was the capital of Australia that Paulo answered?
qa.a: Canberra.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling when he froze?
qa.a: Paulo felt embarrassed after his voice squeaked in front of the class.

qa.q: What helped Paulo laugh it off?
qa.a: Selin ignoring the crack, and Paulo joking about special effects, turned the moment into shared laughter.

qa.q: How did Selin see the voice crack?
qa.a: Selin treated it as unimportant, ignoring it so Paulo wouldn't feel singled out.

grounding: In class, a teenager's voice cracks, a friend ignores it, and he laughs it off instead of going silent.

At the school radio club, Bhupen was reading the morning announcements over the PA system. "Today's lunch is rajma cha—" His voice cracked mid-word, a high squeak through every speaker in the school.
He froze, finger on the button. Asif, the club lead, sat next to him and just gave a calm nod. Keep going.
Bhupen cleared his throat. "Rajma chawal. And that squeak was free of charge."
In the corridor outside, a group of students cheered.
After the broadcast, Asif laughed. "Best announcement this month."
"The whole school heard it," Bhupen groaned.
"And the whole school laughed with you, not at you. That's the difference."

qa.q: What was the lunch announced?
qa.a: Rajma chawal.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when his voice cracked over the speakers?
qa.a: Bhupen felt embarrassed and frozen, knowing the whole school heard it.

qa.q: What helped Bhupen continue the announcement?
qa.a: Asif's calm nod and Bhupen's joke about the squeak helped him laugh it off.

qa.q: How did Asif see the voice crack?
qa.a: Asif treated it as no big deal and saw the joke as making the announcement better.

grounding: On the school radio, a teenager's voice cracks, a friend ignores it, and he laughs it off.
